section_title: How can a widow with almost nothing provide for Elijah?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah: 9 “Get up and go to Zarephath of Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” 10 So Elijah got up and went to Zarephath. When he arrived at the city gate, there was a widow gathering sticks. Elijah called to her and said, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” 11 And as she was going to get it, he called to her and said, “Please bring me a piece of bread.” 12 But she replied, “As surely as the LORD your God lives, I have no bread—only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. Look, I am gathering a couple of sticks to take home and prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.”

13 “Do not be afraid,” Elijah said to her. “Go and do as you have said. But first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me. Afterward, make some for yourself and your son, 14 for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’” 15 So she went and did according to the word of Elijah, and there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household. 16 The jar of flour was not exhausted and the jug of oil did not run dry, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Elijah.

context_lines: God sends Elijah to Zarephath of Sidon and tells him a widow there will provide for him. At the city gate he finds her gathering sticks and asks for water and bread.

Her situation is desperate. She has only a handful of flour and a little oil, enough for what she expects to be a last meal for herself and her son. Elijah tells her not to fear and asks her to make him a small cake first.

The request comes with a specific word from the LORD: her flour and oil will not run out before the rain returns. She acts on that word, and her household and Elijah have food day after day. The provision matches the promise.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/), [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/17.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/17.htm) understand the widow’s response as trust in the promise brought by Elijah. Her lack of resources makes the dependence especially clear.

The promise is essential to the scene. Elijah is not merely demanding that a hungry household feed him without assurance; he brings a word that God will sustain them. That particular promise should govern how the request is understood.
god_plan_lines: Jesus expressly recalls this widow in [Luke 4:24–30](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/4.htm). Speaking in Nazareth, He notes that many widows were in Israel during the famine, yet Elijah was sent to the widow in Zarephath of Sidon.

His example makes the reach of God’s mercy unmistakable. God’s work is not something a hometown or a nation can possess as its exclusive claim. In the larger story, this household outside Israel receives His help, and Jesus uses that history to challenge the expectations of His own hearers.
